overview: Medieval Sardinia was an island of competing kingdoms, farming villages, monasteries and trading towns. Its four giudicati were ruled by sovereigns called judges. The map’s single island-wide colour hides these separate governments and later Pisan, Genoese and Aragonese influence; “Kingdom of Sardinia” is not a suitable description of one continuous island-wide state from 1000 onward.

periods.title: Judges, monasteries and maritime rivals
periods.summary: Four local kingdoms developed amid increasing involvement by Pisa and Genoa.

periods.title: Aragonese expansion and Arborean resistance
periods.summary: Wars transformed the island’s political order; Arborea’s remaining dynastic claims were sold in 1420.

sections.title: Power, work and the wider world

items.text: By the middle of the eleventh century, Cagliari, Arborea, Torres and Gallura were separate kingdoms. Their judges governed territories divided into districts called curatorie. A “judge” here could be a ruler, not simply the person who settled an argument in court.

Rulers donated land and churches to religious communities connected with places as far away as Montecassino and Marseille. Monasteries helped link Sardinia to wider European religious and cultural networks, while Pisa and Genoa pursued commerce and political influence.

Iglesias grew into an important thirteenth-century town beside valuable silver deposits. Mining helped make it a target: Aragonese forces and their Arborean allies besieged the Pisan town in 1323, and it surrendered on 14 January 1324 after seven months.

Reports sent to the Aragonese king in 1308 describe Iglesias enclosed by high battlemented walls and twenty towers. Outside stood a wooden palisade and a ditch, obstacles intended to keep soldiers and siege machines away from the stone defenses.

sections.title: Neighbours, fields and women in the records

items.text: At Geridu, near modern Sorso, excavations expose a rural community’s fourteenth-century surroundings: water, vineyards, vegetable plots, orchards and pasture. Its small buildings clustered around open spaces used for daily activities. Home life spilled outside the front door.

Archaeologists have uncovered more than fifteen homes near Geridu’s church, cemetery and a larger privileged building. Written records mention the village in 1112. Its population declined from the mid-fourteenth century, and it was abandoned by 1427; the excavated village is a particular community, not a model for every Sardinian home.

The condaghi, monastery record books, preserve purchases, disputes and people who otherwise might disappear from history. At the women’s monastery of San Pietro di Silki, abbesses administered property. These books particularly record cases the institution won or settled, so the monastery’s voice is louder than its opponents’ voices.

The same records reveal sharp limits to freedom. Abbesses could participate in exchanges of unfree people, and some exchanges were annulled because the ruler’s permission was missing. A woman holding authority in a monastery did not mean that all women, or all families, controlled their own lives.

Saccargia’s church belonged to the Camaldolese monks by 1112. Its contrasting light and dark stonework makes the building striking from outside; Romanesque paintings survive in its apse inside. Skilled builders and painters made religious spaces into some of the island’s most lasting medieval achievements.

In the late fourteenth century, Eleonora of Arborea promulgated the Carta de Logu. It combined civil and criminal rules with rural legislation developed under her father, Mariano IV. The law used an Arborean form of Sardinian and remained influential long after her kingdom disappeared.

A tiny sample of its written language is “Nos Elianora”, meaning “We, Eleonora”. These are words from the prologue, shown here in a modern transcription of the historic Sardinian text. The ruler explains that her subjects should know the rules by which they are expected to live.

Article 86 addressed dishonest measures and weighing scales. An official who found a false measure could trigger a fine payable within fifteen days, with corporal punishment for failure to pay. Shopping already had a familiar problem: was the seller really giving you the promised amount?

Article 87 prohibited taking goshawks or falcons from their nests. The district official had to bring an offender before the ruler. These birds mattered to elite hunting, so this protection should not be mistaken for a modern wildlife conservation programme.

ending.text: Arborea’s defeat at Sanluri in 1409 and the sale of its remaining dynastic rights in 1420 marked decisive steps in Aragonese consolidation. Sardinia’s people, villages and laws continued under new rulers. The map’s 1492 cutoff is a coverage boundary, not the disappearance of the island or its society.
